title: Different boxes. Shared ingredients?
summary: See why differently named medicines can share an ingredient, and what to clarify with your pharmacist.
narration: Different medicine names can hide a shared active ingredient. These boxes are fictional, not real medicines.
Read every ingredient. A combination product contains several. Both boxes list X.
A shared ingredient flags possible overlap. It does not decide medicine changes.
Both boxes list X. What does that tell you?
Possible overlap needs a pharmacist or prescriber's clarification. This lesson cannot decide medicine changes.
Bring packaging and prescriptions. Explain actual use. This is general education only.

checkpoint.prompt: Two different boxes both list ingredient X. What can you conclude?

choices.feedback: Yes. A shared ingredient is a review flag, not a decision to stop, combine, or change medicines.

choices.text: Different brand names rule out overlap.
choices.feedback: Names alone do not rule out overlap. Compare all active ingredients and ask for professional clarification.

choices.text: The two products must be interchangeable.
choices.feedback: A shared ingredient does not establish interchangeability. Strength, formulation, and instructions also matter.

title: One label. How many servings?
summary: Understand the difference between the amount on a label and the portion on your plate.
narration: This fictional label lists twelve grams of carbohydrate per thirty gram serving. Start with that reference amount.
The portion shown weighs sixty grams. Dividing sixty by thirty gives two label servings, not one.
Each serving has twelve grams of carbohydrate. Two equal servings contain twice that amount.
Twelve grams per serving. How much in two servings? Choose now.
Twelve times two equals twenty four grams. These invented numbers explain the method, not a particular food.
Serving size is not a recommendation. Check for per serving, per package, or per hundred grams.

checkpoint.prompt: 12 g carbohydrate per 30 g serving: how much is in a 60 g portion?

choices.feedback: 12 g is for one 30 g serving. This 60 g portion contains two servings.
Correct: 60 ÷ 30 = 2 servings, then 12 × 2 = 24 g carbohydrate. This is label arithmetic, not a glucose prediction.
60 g is the whole food's mass, not its carbohydrate amount. Multiply the carbohydrate per serving by two.

title: An empty log is not an answer.
summary: What to do with an uncertain record—without guessing whether another dose is needed.
narration: A reminder was sent, but the log is empty. That does not establish whether a medicine was taken.
Reminders, reports, and actual intake are different things. Keep the time and source of reports visible.
If memory and records disagree, preserve the uncertainty. An app entry is not proof that medicine was swallowed.
Checkpoint. No entry, and the person is unsure. What should the record say?
Record unsure, with source and time. Ask a pharmacist about uncertainty, not an app.
For suspected overdose or severe symptoms, seek urgent local medical help. Do not wait for an app review.

checkpoint.prompt: The log is empty and the person cannot remember. Which record is supported?

choices.feedback: A missing entry does not prove a missed medicine. Keep the uncertainty visible.
There is not enough evidence to mark it taken. Preserve the person's uncertainty.
Yes. Record what is known without inventing certainty. Seek professional guidance, not an app-generated dose decision.

title: From your meal to your muscle cells
summary: Follow digestion, the pancreas and insulin signalling through a labelled biological schematic.
narration: Digestion releases glucose into blood. The liver can also supply glucose.
The pancreas makes insulin, a hormone. This diagram is not to scale.
Blood carries glucose and insulin. Insulin signalling helps muscle cells take up glucose.
What does insulin help the body do? Pause and choose in the player.
In type two diabetes, cells respond less well. Insulin may also be insufficient.
Discuss patterns with your care team. This diagram cannot choose medicine doses.

checkpoint.prompt: What role does insulin have in this diagram?

choices.text: It helps signal glucose uptake into cells.
choices.feedback: Yes. Insulin is a hormone that helps the body use and store glucose. The drawing is a simplified process, not a personal prediction.

choices.text: It removes all carbohydrate from food.
choices.feedback: Digestion breaks down carbohydrate. Insulin is a hormone involved in how the body handles glucose, not a way to remove carbohydrate from a meal.

choices.text: It tells the app which dose to choose.
choices.feedback: This explanation cannot determine a medicine dose. Your treating professional guides treatment.
